common_name: King Alfred Daffodil (Classic Large Golden Trumpet Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; King Alfred is the archetypal large trumpet daffodil that popularized the type, though in zone 9 daffodils generally do not perennialize reliably due to insufficient winter chilling and are often best treated as an annual spring bulb display or pre-chilled purchase.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil, and allow foliage to yellow and die back naturally after bloom rather than cutting or braiding it, since the leaves recharge the bulb for next year's flowers. King Alfred is the name most people associate with the classic golden daffodil, a large-trumpet type with a long, flaring, deep yellow trumpet surrounded by broad yellow petals, made famous in the early 1900s as one of the first daffodils widely sold and planted at scale. True original King Alfred stock has become rare in commerce and much of what is sold under the name today is actually a similar, very close modern strain, but the bold golden trumpet form it popularized remains the benchmark image of a classic daffodil. It naturalizes well in climates with sufficient winter chill and is completely deer- and rodent-resistant.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Daffodil Varieties for Gulf South Gardens

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; Tete-a-Tete is a popular miniature daffodil often forced for winter and early spring container color, and in zone 9 it may be best treated as an annual display bulb rather than a reliable long-term perennial.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. Tete-a-Tete is one of the most widely grown miniature daffodils, valued for its small stature, early bloom, and habit of producing two or more small, bright golden-yellow flowers per stem, giving a cheerful, multiplied display from each bulb. Its compact size makes it especially popular for containers, rock gardens, and small-space plantings, and it is often sold as a potted, forced bulb for indoor winter color as well as an outdoor garden plant. Like other daffodils it is completely resistant to deer and rodents, and foliage should be allowed to yellow and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Daffodil Varieties for Gulf South Gardens

common_name: February Gold Daffodil (Early-Blooming Miniature Cyclamineus Daffodil)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in fall in well-drained soil; February Gold is one of the earliest daffodils to bloom, often flowering in late winter well ahead of most other cultivars, giving an early splash of color in the shade garden's dormant season.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in well-drained, moderately fertile soil. February Gold is a Cyclamineus-type daffodil, recognizable by its swept-back petals and long trumpet that give the flower a distinctive windblown look, and it is prized above all for being one of the very earliest daffodils to bloom, often opening its golden-yellow flowers in late winter well before most other cultivars have even emerged. Its smaller, more graceful proportions compared to large trumpet types make it a good fit for naturalizing under deciduous trees and shrubs, where it gets adequate sun before the canopy leafs out. It multiplies reliably in climates with sufficient winter chill and, like all daffodils, is completely resistant to deer and rodents.
sources: Louisiana State University AgCenter — Daffodil Varieties for Gulf South Gardens

common_name: Australia Canna (Dark Purple-Black Foliage Red-Flowered Canna)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Australia is grown chiefly for its striking near-black glossy foliage, which holds its dark color best in full sun.

directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season for the best foliage color and flowering. Australia is a dramatic canna cultivar grown primarily for its glossy, deep maroon-black leaves, among the darkest of any commonly available canna, which serve as a bold foil for its clear red summer flowers and for brighter-colored companion plants nearby. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder that wants consistent moisture but sharp drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground through zone 9 and warmer, expanding into a larger clump each year that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones the rhizomes can be lifted after the first frost kills the foliage and stored dry over winter.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canna Growing Guide

common_name: Bengal Tiger Canna (Yellow-and-Green Striped Foliage Orange-Flowered Canna)

planting.note: Divide rhizomes in early spring and plant in rich, moist, well-drained soil once soil has warmed; Bengal Tiger is grown for its bold yellow-and-green striped foliage, which colors most vividly in full sun.

directions: Plant rhizomes a few inches deep in rich, consistently moist, well-amended soil in full sun, feeding monthly during the growing season for the strongest foliage color and flowering. Bengal Tiger produces bold, paddle-shaped leaves striped lengthwise in vivid yellow and green, similar in effect to the more red-toned Tropicanna but with a brighter, more citrus-toned color scheme, topped with bright orange summer flowers that pick up the warm tones of the foliage. Like other cannas it is a heavy feeder needing consistent moisture and excellent drainage to avoid rhizome rot, and it overwinters reliably in the ground in zone 9 and warmer, forming an expanding clump that benefits from periodic division. In colder zones, lift rhizomes after the first killing frost and store them dry over winter.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Canna Growing Guide
